speaker_role: consultant/content creator (College Essay Guy) featuring an on-camera current admissions officer (assistant VP of admissions, Southwestern University)
commercial_incentive: yes - College Essay Guy sells essay-writing guides/services and promotes its site throughout
key_insights: Colleges track demonstrated interest through CRM-style dashboards that log email opens/clicks, event attendance, and website visits, shown on-camera by a Southwestern University admissions officer.
Demonstrated interest tracking is tied to yield (enrolled/accepted ratio), which affects enrollment planning and factors into US News rankings.
Students can check whether a specific school tracks demonstrated interest by searching '[school name] + common data set' and looking at the 'level of applicant's interest' row in Section C.

Low-lift ways to build a interest trail: join the school's email list and actually click links, create an account/portal if offered, attend a college fair and get your badge scanned, visit in person or virtually, interview if offered, and apply ED/EA.
Spending real time on supplemental 'why us' essays is described as possibly the most useful demonstrated-interest signal available.
Demonstrated interest tends to matter more at smaller colleges than at huge schools like UCLA, and college fair reps will often honestly answer if asked directly whether their school tracks it.
Doing nothing about demonstrated interest is presented as a completely acceptable option for students without time/energy for it.
specific_numbers_or_facts: UCLA is cited as an example of a school that lists demonstrated interest as 'not considered' on its common data set (per video)
Bates is cited as an example of a school that lists it as 'considered' or 'important' (per video)
notable_or_distinctive: Shows an actual admissions CRM dashboard on screen (via a real admissions officer) with color-coded interest tracking, which is a rarely-seen concrete illustration of how demonstrated interest is recorded internally.
reliability_notes: Generally reliable and sourced from a named current admissions officer, but framed within a promotional video for the host's paid essay-writing services; some claims (e.g., which schools care most) are generalizations from the host's experience rather than data.
